newsitem.title: USA: Lake's pullout a political black eye for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Lake's pullout a political black eye for Clinton.

text.p: Tony Lake's decision to give up his fight to be CIA director is a major setback for President Bill Clinton and hard evidence of the corrosive effect that campaign finance controversies are having on Clinton and his team.
A quiet, unpretentious man in a town filled with oversized egos, Lake said in a two-page letter to Clinton he no longer wished to be "a political football in a game with constantly moving goal posts"

Lake, 57, who was Clinton's first-term national security adviser, had been grilled by Republicans about his financial transactions, his role in formulating U.S. policy toward Bosnia and Haiti, and his failure to thwart suspected foreign efforts to buy influence in the Clinton White House.

When it became clear Lake had been kept "out of the loop" on the campaign fundraising practices of freewheeling Clinton re-election operatives, his critics accused him of lacking the kind of management skills necessary to run the complex, far-flung U.S. intelligence network.

"I have gone through the past three months and more with patience and, I hope, dignity. But I have lost the former and and could lose the latter as this political circus continues indefinitely," Lake said in his letter to the president.

The withdrawal of his nomination left a big hole in Clinton's national security team as he prepared for his Helsinki summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin this Thursday and Friday, and a flurry of other international forays in the near future including trips to Mexico and Latin America.

Because of this, the White House signalled that Clinton would swiftly name Lake's replacement. Officials said deputy CIA director George Tenet, who once served as staff director of the Senate Intellience Committee, was a leading candidate.

Lake's forced exit also made a shambles of Clinton's dream of a new spirit of bipartisanship between the Democratic White House and the Republican Congress that would end the political paralysis that has gripped the government in recent years.

"All of us here at the White House really hope people will read Tony Lake's letter carefully, and think about what it says about the town that we live in and the way we do business," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
McCurry said Lake, who also served in Richard Nixon's White House and Jimmy Carter's State Department, was the victim of an "inexcusably flawed" confirmation process.

Some wondered if Lake had gotten sufficient support from a White House -- and a president -- notorious for fumbling nominations. But Samuel Berger, who succeed Lake as national security adviser, said little more could have been done.

"I think there's been no question about the commitment of the White House and the commitment of this president to Tony's confirmation," Berger told reporters. "The president believes very, very deeply today no less than the day he made the selection that Tony was the right person to lead the CIA."

White House sources said a contributing factor in Lake's decision to throw in the towel was the latest disclosure in the mushrooming Clinton campaign financing controversy: that the Democratic National Committee overrode the objections of the National Security Council, then run by Lake, to letting a Lebanese-American businessman attend several White House functions where Clinton was present.
The CIA has begun an internal probe into whether the DNC made "improper contacts and inquiries" with the agency on behalf of the businessman, acting director Tenet said Monday.

But this is only the latest in a string of disclosures about aggressive Democratic fund-raising practices. They have raised serious questions of influence-peddling and are under both Justice Department and congressional investigation.
Clinton has strongly defended those practices and blamed excesses on the money-gobbling U.S. political system, which he says is "out of whack."

But Lake, caught in the middle of a controversy he claimed to play no part in, may come to be regarded as the first casualty of a 1996 Clinton re-election campaign that pushed that system to the limit.
